items.passage:
51 | 
52 | The TUI and CLI are equivalent — anything you can do in the TUI, you can do with [CLI commands](/using-syllago/cli-reference/). The TUI is for interactive exploration; the CLI is for scripting and automation (`--json` output on all commands).
53 |

reviews.rationale: 'CLI' contrasted with 'TUI' is standard technical terminology in developer documentation.
'CLI' noun; rewrite as 'command-line interface.'
This is a product category label, not forbidden wording.
CLI is used generically throughout; “command-line interface” or “command-line tool” would be clearer.
Standard concise technical heading ('Use with CLI tools:').
'CLI tools' rewritable as 'command-line tools.'
This is a product category label, not forbidden wording.
“CLI tools” is generic jargon; “command-line tools” follows the prescribed terminology.

items.rule_summary: Avoid time-based words like 'latest' in product documentation.
items.passage:
36 | 
37 | Sync periodically to pull the latest content:
38 |

reviews.rationale: 'Latest content' refers accurately to git/registry sync, not an ephemeral time reference.
Time-based word; Google style avoids temporal language in product docs.
This generic instruction can avoid time-dependent wording by describing synchronization without “latest.”
Here “latest” identifies the changing remote content that synchronization retrieves.

items.passage: Filesystem. The sandboxed process can only see your current working directory. The rest of the filesystem is hidden. This prevents AI-generated code from reading or modifying files outside the project.

reviews.rationale: Describing a process as able to 'see' files attributes human senses to software.
'Can see' and 'hidden' are idiomatic technical language for filesystem access restrictions, not misleading anthropomorphism.
Software 'seeing' is conventional in sandbox contexts; this is borderline.
“Access” states the filesystem restriction more precisely than saying the process can “see.”

items.passage: This starts the provider with filesystem, network, and env var restrictions active. The provider works normally from the user's perspective, but its access is constrained to what you've allowed.

reviews.rationale: Refers to the reader inconsistently as 'the user' alongside second-person 'you'.
Passage mixes indirect and direct address; includes 'you've allowed' but opens with passive 'This starts'; mixed approach.
The reader is directly addressed and the sentence is compliant.
“The user's perspective” inconsistently shifts away from the reader addressed as “you.”

items.passage: This means team standards can evolve from the bottom up. Individual developers experiment locally, and the best content gets published to the shared registry for everyone.

reviews.rationale: Avoid standalone 'This' as a pronoun without a clarifying noun referent.
Pronouns 'this' and 'the best content' have reasonably clear referents despite density; contextually interpretable.
The antecedent is clear and the sentence doesn't mislead.
The referent of “This” can only be judged from preceding context.

items.passage: The registry is the source of truth. Loadouts make it easy to apply. Project config ties it to specific repos. CI keeps everything in sync automatically.

reviews.rationale: 'Make it easy' is a minimizing claim; Google style discourages using 'easy'.
Architectural claims about registry, loadouts, and CI sync are design assertions; acceptable for architecture documentation but lack supporting evidence.
This is a strong product summary, but it remains supported.
“Easy” is a minimizing usability claim unsupported by the passage.

items.passage: This page covers the four concepts that make the rest of the docs make sense: providers, content types, collections, and format conversion.

reviews.rationale: Google style discourages meta-openings like 'This page covers'; start topics directly with core information.
Sentence immediately lists the four concepts; not pre-announcing but providing a roadmap, which aids readability.
This page overview is ordinary framing, not a pre-announcement problem.
“This page covers” pre-announces the content instead of presenting it directly.

items.passage: Follow the terminal prompts: [code] detects the AI coding tools (providers) on your machine and asks you to confirm which ones to manage. In the provider picker, space toggles a selection and enter confirms. When it finishes, your config exists at [code]. To skip the prompts and accept defaults, pass [code].

reviews.rationale: Google style discourages software 'asking'; rewriting to 'prompts you to confirm' improves style.
Mild anthropomorphism in 'asks'; common but stylistic preference varies. Recoverable from context.
CLI prompts routinely use agent-like descriptions without misleading personification.
“Detects” and “asks” clearly describe automated behavior and a displayed confirmation prompt.

items.passage: Add Roo Code, Cline, Amp, Gemini CLI, Codex, OpenCode, Zed, Factory Droid, Crush, and Pi, and the table grows in every dimension. MCP servers compound it — each client wires them up its own way.

reviews.rationale: 'It' lacks a clear singular antecedent, referring vaguely to the overall complexity or table growth.
Pronoun 'its' slightly ambiguous (client vs. table) but recoverable from context.
The antecedents are clear: 'it' is complexity; 'them' are MCP servers.
In “compound it,” the pronoun vaguely refers to complexity inferred from earlier discussion, not a clear noun.

items.rule_summary: Use present tense for current behavior
items.passage: Compatibility checking. [[code]](/using-syllago/cli-reference/compat/) reports which providers can fully consume an item and where features will degrade in translation, so you know before you publish.

reviews.rationale: 'Will degrade' should be present tense ('degrade') to describe ongoing tool behavior.
'Will degrade' is conditional future describing current feature capability, not unnecessary.
'Will degrade' describes a translation outcome; present tense is less precise here.
“Will degrade” describes a predicted consequence of a later translation, making future tense meaningful.

items.rule_summary: Use present tense for current behavior
items.passage: The cost curve bends as tools and teammates multiply. Every copy is a chance to drift: you fix a rule in Claude Code and forget the Cursor version, a provider renames its config directory and your shell script silently writes to the old one, two teammates "share" a rule that diverged three edits ago. Syllago replaces N copies with one canonical item plus conversion, so an edit lands everywhere and [[code]](/using-syllago/cli-reference/compat/) tells you where translation will degrade.

reviews.rationale: 'Will degrade' is unnecessary future tense; present tense 'degrades' should be used.
'Will degrade' describes conditional capability, not unnecessary future tense.
The future tense refers to translation consequences and reads as a product capability.
The compatibility command predicts degradation that would occur during translation, so future tense is justified.

items.passage: The syllago TUI interface exposes a reusable Trust Inspector modal that renders the full trust story for either an item or a whole registry. The same modal serves both scopes so the user sees a consistent shape regardless of where they opened it from.

reviews.rationale: Refers to 'the user' and 'they' instead of addressing the reader directly as 'you'.
Third-person describes system behavior. Could prefer 'you'll see', but context-dependent.
The sentence stays objective and avoids second-person address.
“The user” refers to the reader indirectly; second-person “you” would be clearer and more direct.

items.passage: Or create one manually — a registry is just a git repo with syllago's content structure:

reviews.rationale: 'Just' is a minimizing word that should be avoided per Google style guidelines.
'Just a git repo' encourages simplicity, not excessive. Helpful framing, not minimizing.
'Just' is explanatory, not a minimizing or unsupported claim.
“Just” minimizes registry requirements, even though the required content structure makes the qualification important.

Choose violation, not_violation, or uncertain. Resolve reviewer mistakes rather than voting mechanically. Use uncertain only for a genuine policy choice or insufficient context. For semantic_gap items, also decide whether ordinary deterministic Vale/regex logic can reliably make the decision. Keep each rationale under 24 words. Return every id exactly once.
